The dry run prints every remote command and every local ssh config or
known-hosts change and changes nothing. The real run uses the human's admin
ssh session and passwordless `sudo`; it generates or reuses only the hub key
`~/.ssh/pulse_hands_ed25519`, never a personal key, inspects before any
change, and applies one idempotent setup: a locked `pulse` user,
`/usr/local/bin/pulse-hands`, a 0750 workdir, exactly one restricted
`authorized_keys` line, the sshd drop-in
`/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/60-pulse-hands.conf`, git `commit.gpgsign false`,
and `core.askPass ""`. With `--install-copilot`, it installs Node.js 22 and
`@github/copilot` on apt systems only; on any other system that flag is a
refusal.

The sshd step is built to keep the admin path open. `pair` writes the drop-in,
runs `sshd -t`, and removes the drop-in without reloading when the check
fails. After a clean check it reloads sshd and opens a second admin
connection; if that connection fails, the held admin session removes the
drop-in and reloads again. Refusals exit 2 with nothing changed: non-Linux,
no passwordless sudo, an existing `authorized_keys` for `pulse` with any
other line, no `sshd_config.d`, a clone with a remote under the workdir, a
conflicting `Host <executor>` alias, or an executor of that name already tied
to another address.

After the remote side is safe, `pair` writes the local `Host <executor>` alias
with `IdentitiesOnly yes`, trusts the host key through the admin session, runs
`executor add <executor> --ssh pulse@<executor>`, and probes. The store sees
the alias, not the address.

The copilot login is a separate human credential step from the hub:

```bash
op read 'op://Vault/item/field' | python3 docs/scripts/pulse.py executor login vm1 --admin admin@host --with-token
python3 docs/scripts/pulse.py executor login vm1 --admin admin@host --remove
```

`executor login` reads one token from standard input only (`github_pat_`,
`gho_`, or `ghu_`; classic `ghp_` is refused because the CLI rejects it),
first writes the storage consent as user `pulse` - a headless machine has no
keychain, and the CLI's "store in plaintext?" question is answered no for
itself when standard input is a pipe, so the token would validate and then
be thrown away; `storeTokenPlaintext: true` in `~pulse/.copilot/settings.json`
(700/600, merged if the file has other keys) is that consent given in
advance, and the token stays home if this step fails - then pipes it to
`sudo -u pulse -H copilot login --with-token`, redacts token-shaped output,
records only `executor.login` with the executor name, token kind (`pat`,
`oauth`, `user`, or `removed`), and exit code, then probes and runs the
**login check** below; only a passing check re-activates an executor the
runner had drained for its login. `--remove` deletes `~pulse/.copilot`
because the CLI has no logout, then probes and leaves the executor drained.
A `~/.copilot` holding only `logs/` or only `settings.json` is not a login;
the probe requires a login record in `config.json` (non-empty `authTokens`
or `loggedInUsers`) or a token in `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN`, `GH_TOKEN`, or
`GITHUB_TOKEN`.

### A stored login is not a working one: the login check

`copilot login --with-token` only asks GitHub who the token belongs to. A
fine-grained token **without the "Copilot Requests" permission**, or an
account without Copilot, logs in fine and is refused at the first real
request (`Authentication failed … ensure it has the 'Copilot Requests'
permission`) - pulse-vm1 sat `drained` for a day in 2026-09 with
`logged_in=yes` in every probe. So the truth is one real call
([WU-016](../plans/WU-016-executor-login-check.md)):

- **Before the token leaves your machine** `executor login` asks GitHub
  about it (`GET /user`, the token in the header, nothing logged): a refused
  token (401/403) is never sent, an accepted one records the account name
  and the expiry GitHub reports in the `executor.login` event, and an expiry
  within seven days prints a warning. When GitHub cannot be reached the
  token is sent anyway and the fact is marked unknown.
- **After the token is stored** the hub runs the same verbs a job uses -
  `prepare` a one-commit clone, `run` the copilot CLI with the worker model
  and a one-word prompt (`--no-ask-user --disable-builtin-mcps -s`, two
  minutes), `clean` - and records `executor.login-check` with `ok`, `kind`
  (`ok`, `refused`, `failed`, `hands`, `unreachable`), and the copilot
  line that names the fault. `pulse executor probe vm1 --login` runs it by
  hand; the plain `probe` of a machine drained for its login includes it.
- **A refused login drains the machine and schedules its own recovery**:
  `fault: copilot refuses the login …` in `probe_note`, `backoff_minutes`
  15, `next_probe_at`. The daemon runs the login check again when it is due
  (15, 30, 60 … minutes, at most every six hours) and, the moment it passes -
  because the token's permissions were fixed on GitHub, or a new token was
  placed with `executor login` - sets the machine `active` by itself
  (`executor.recovered`). A shallow probe that passes keeps such a machine
  drained: `logged_in=yes` only says a login is stored. `pulse executor
  list` shows the last check and the known expiry under each machine.

## Enroll, probe, run

```bash
python3 docs/scripts/pulse.py executor add vm1 --ssh pulse@vm1 --workdir /srv/pulse --workers 1 --projects '*'   # the ssh alias, not an address
python3 docs/scripts/pulse.py executor probe vm1      # activates it when every check passes
python3 docs/scripts/pulse.py executor list           # local + vm1, status, slots, runs, last probe
python3 docs/scripts/pulse.py work --dry-run --executor vm1   # bundle over, clone there, brief written, no worker, cleaned
python3 docs/scripts/pulse.py work --executor vm1     # one real job there
python3 docs/scripts/pulse.py status                  # the executors line the daemon also reads
```

`add` registers the machine **drained**: it takes no job until a probe
passes. The probe connects with `BatchMode=yes`, `ConnectTimeout=15`, and
`ClearAllForwardings=yes` and asks the hands to report; it passes only when

| Field | Must be |
| --- | --- |
| `hands` | `ok` - the forced command answered |
| `user` | the single-purpose user |
| `workdir` | exactly the `--workdir` you registered (absolute) |
| `git`, `copilot` | present with a version (`missing` fails) |
| `logged_in` | `yes` - `~/.copilot/config.json` records a login (non-empty `authTokens` for a plaintext store or `loggedInUsers` for a keychain) or the CLI's token variable is set; a fresh machine, one with only `logs/` from a failed login, or one holding only the `settings.json` consent says `no` |
| `remotes` | `0` - no clone under the work directory has a remote (a leftover with one is a finding, not a job host) |
| `keys_ok` | `yes` - every `authorized_keys` line for that user carries `command=` and `restrict` |
| `disk_free_mb` | at least 1024 |
| `jobs` | job directories still present (`-` when none); informational - a passing probe sweeps the idle ones |
| `keys` | job directories still holding a `run.key` (`-` when none); one whose run is not `running` and that the sweep did not remove fails the probe (`N signing key(s) left without a live run`) |

The note is stored (`probe_note`) and shown by `list`, `status`, and the
dashboard's Agents page. `activate` refuses an executor whose last probe
failed; run `probe` again after fixing the machine. The daemon needs no
restart: it reads the executors each loop and fills every free slot
(remote hands limited to some projects lease first, `local` is the
fallback), running the leased jobs in parallel and printing one line per
run, `done <job> <agent> on vm1: <summary>`.

## When to add a machine

A machine costs money and carries a Copilot login, so adding one is always
the human's act; the runner's part is to say, with numbers, when one would
help ([WU-019](../plans/WU-019-runner-throughput.md)):

- **Read the wait first.** `pulse status` prints a `capacity` line while
  jobs are queued: `N job(s) queued, S slot(s), F in flight; every slot busy
  for M min - another machine would help`.
  Slots idle beside a queue means the *dispatch rules* are the limit, not
  the hardware - raise `parallel_per_project` (one project may then run
  more than one job at once; ADR-024 landing merges the branches and
  requeues real conflicts with a patch) before pairing anything.
- **Let the daemon ask.** After every slot has been busy for
  `HANDS_WANTED_MINUTES` (30) with work still queued, the daemon posts one
  `finding` a day on the brain's board, area `runner`, thread
  `hands-wanted`, with the queue, slot, and in-flight counts and the three
  answers: pair a machine, raise `workers` where a machine has spare cores,
  or raise `parallel_per_project`. It is data for you, never an instruction;
  it never buys, provisions, or pairs anything.
- **Then pair.** Follow "Provision a machine" or "Pair a machine that
  already exists" above, place the token with `pulse executor login <name>
  --admin <admin@host> --with-token`, and the daemon fills the new slots on
  its next tick - no restart, no setting to flip.
- **What stays yours:** the money, the credential, `jobs_per_day` and the
  other caps, and the merge of what the extra hands produce.

## What a machine needs installed

A throwaway clone has no dependencies, so before the worker starts and
before every check the runner installs exactly what the project's lockfile
pins ([WU-021](../plans/WU-021-runnable-clones.md)): `uv.lock` → `uv sync
--frozen --all-extras`, `poetry.lock` → `poetry install`, `pnpm-lock.yaml` →
`corepack pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `yarn.lock` → `corepack yarn
install --frozen-lockfile`, `package-lock.json` → `npm ci`, `bun.lock` →
`bun install --frozen-lockfile`, `go.sum` → `go mod download`, `Cargo.lock`
→ `cargo fetch`, `Gemfile.lock` → `bundle install`, `composer.lock` →
`composer install` - the first lockfile of each ecosystem at the repository
root of the base commit, joined with `&&`, non-interactive. The worker never
installs anything itself and a branch that edits a lockfile is checked
against the default branch's copy: dependencies stay Tier 2.

The *tools* those commands need are the machine's, and installing one is
your act:

- **What the runner does when a tool is missing.** The setup ends
  `command not found`; the run is an `error`, the job goes back to the queue
  with its attempt returned, and the machine is marked *unfit for that
  project only* (`meta.unfit`) for 24 hours - it keeps serving every other
  project and is never drained for this. The same mark follows a check that
  cannot start after the worker ran (`make: command not found`): that run
  fails - unverified commits never land - and the job returns to the queue
  for a machine that can judge it. `pulse status` shows `pulse-vm1
  active (0/1 busy); lacks uv for project-light`, and once a day per machine
  and tool the daemon posts one `finding` on the brain's board, area
  `runner`, thread `tools-wanted`, with the install line. Data for you, never
  an instruction.
- **Install, then probe.** On the machine, as the executor user unless the
  line says `sudo`:
  - `uv`: `curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh` (lands in
    `~/.local/bin`, which the hands put on PATH; refresh hands older than
    WU-021 with `pulse pair <admin@host> --name <name>` first)
  - `make`: `sudo apt-get install -y make` (a `make test` check needs it
    even when the lockfile is `uv.lock`)
  - Node tooling: `corepack` ships with the Node 22 that `pulse pair`
    installs alongside `@github/copilot`; `pnpm`/`yarn` download through it
    on first use
  - `poetry`, `bun`, `cargo`, `go`, `bundle`, `composer`: the `finding`
    prints the line for each
  Then on the hub: `pulse executor probe <name>`. A **human** probe clears
  the machine's unfit marks (the daemon's own rechecks do not, so a machine
  is not retried every few minutes); the project's next job may run there
  again.
- **The provisioning template** (`docs/scripts/hosted/`) installs git,
  Python 3, Node 22, the Copilot CLI, and a pinned `mise` (the version and
  checksum live in `pulse.py`; `pulse pair` installs the same one and its
  inspect step prints `mise=<version|missing>`). Add `make` and `uv` to a
  new machine when a Python project is on the hub and its recipe does not
  pin them.

## The project's environment recipe

A project says what its clones need in one file at the root of its own
tree, `docs/context/environment.md`
([ADR-026](../decisions/ADR-026-project-environment-recipes.md),
[PLAN-026](../plans/PLAN-026-project-environment-recipes.md), template
`docs/context/_template-environment.md`). `pulse onboard` scaffolds it once
and never overwrites it; the onboarding job's brief asks the agent to fill
it from the checkout and commit it alone. The runner reads it **at the base
commit of the job**, so a branch cannot change what its own check runs with.

- **`tools`** - up to twelve exact `name@version` pins (`node@22.1.0`,
  `uv@0.8.3`; never `latest`). Before setup the runner runs
  `mise install <pins>` with `MISE_YES=1` and the clone's own mise files
  ignored, then wraps setup, worker, and check in `mise exec <pins> --`.
  No `mise` on the machine → the machine is unfit for the project (`lacks
  mise`); a pin mise cannot install → `lacks <pin>`, with a `finding` on
  `runner/tools-wanted` as for any missing tool. Pins wait for **hands that
  can take them**: remote hands from before this change are `hands
  outdated` for a project with `tools` or `env` until `pulse pair` refreshes
  them; the hub itself takes pins from the first run.
- **`setup`** - the exact commands for the clone. Present, it replaces the
  lockfile heuristic above; `setup: []` runs nothing on purpose; absent, the
  heuristic decides as before. The runner runs it non-interactively, joined
  with `&&`, before the worker and before every check.
- **`env`** - names and plain values exported for setup, worker, and check
  (`CI: "1"`, a path, a feature flag). Names that look like secrets
  (`TOKEN`, `SECRET`, `PASSWORD`, `_KEY`, `CREDENTIAL`, `PRIVATE`) and values
  shaped like one (a key block, `://user:pass@`, a JWT, an opaque forty-char
  run) make the recipe **invalid**; a secret's home is the machine's
  keychain, never this file. Briefs, findings, and `pulse env check` print
  variable *names*, never values.
- **`services`** - anything the clone would need running beside it
  (`postgres`, `redis`). A non-empty list keeps the project off every
  machine before a job is spent (`needs services`) until a later slice
  provides them or the owner empties the list.
- **`suggested_check`** - what the owner would run; the store's
  `verify_cmd` still decides, and `pulse env check` shows both side by side.

An **invalid recipe** ends every job for the project as an `error` before a
worker starts (the job returns to the queue, one `finding` a day on the
project's `runner/environment` thread names the problem, event
`env.invalid`) until an owner fixes it. A branch that **changes the recipe
travels alone**: with any other file it is refused (`recipe changes travel
alone`); alone, agent landing holds it (`held`), one `question` on
`runner/environment` carries the diff, and only a human lands it with
`pulse land --project <slug> --branch <branch>` (with no `PULSE_AGENT` set;
an agent naming the branch is still held). The landing check runs with the
base's recipe, exactly like a lockfile change.

`pulse env check [--project P] [--executor E] [--json]` reads it all
without installing or marking anything: the recipe at the tip of each
default branch (valid, or `INVALID` with the problems), the held branches
that wait for you, and per machine whether it can serve the project now
(`lacks mise`, `lacks <pin>`, `needs services`, `hands outdated`, or the
lockfile heuristic's program missing on this machine). Exit `1` when any
machine is unfit, so a shell can gate on it.

## Watch, drain, remove

- **Daemon log** (`~/.pulse/logs/daemon.log`): `error <job> … on vm1:
  executor vm1 unreachable before worker start` means ssh failed before the
  worker began - the job is requeued and nothing was spent; `failed … on
  vm1: executor vm1 unreachable after worker start` means contact was lost
  mid-run - the cap was spent and the job fails after its attempts run out;
  `executor vm1 is reachable again: ok: …` closes an outage.
- **Unreachable.** Three transport errors in a row set `status =
  unreachable`; the daemon skips the machine and re-probes with a doubling
  wait (1, 2, 4 minutes … capped at its interval or an hour). A passing
  probe - the daemon's or yours - brings it back with the counters reset.
- **Faults - the machine answered, and the answer means a human must fix
  it** ([WU-014](../plans/WU-014-executor-faults-are-the-machines.md)):
  hands that refuse a verb this hub needs (`verb not allowed: key` - they
  predate the hub; `pulse pair <admin@host> --name vm1` refreshes them) or
  a worker rejected at launch for its login (`re-authenticate`, `not logged
  in`, `Copilot Requests` … - `pulse executor login vm1 --admin
  <admin@host> --with-token`). The run ends `error` naming the command, the
  machine goes `drained` with `fault: …` in its `probe_note`
  (`executor.drained` event), and the job returns to the queue **with its
  attempt returned** - a machine fault never counts toward the three runner
  errors that fail a job - so the next loop runs it on `local` or on other
  hands. A login fault also seeds the recovery wait: the daemon reruns the
  login check (15, 30, 60 … minutes, capped at six hours) and re-activates
  the machine by itself when it passes. For every other fault only a human
  probe that passes (`probe`, `pair`, or `login`) re-activates the machine;
  the probe itself fails hands without a `keys=` field, so an upgraded hub
  names every machine left behind. On `local` there is no row to drain: a
  login failure there is charged like any runner error and shows in the
  daemon log.
- **Drain** (`pulse executor drain vm1`) stops new leases and lets the
  running job finish. **Remove** (`pulse executor remove vm1`) is refused
  while a run is on it; drain first. Both are events; the machine's runs
  stay in `runs` with `executor = vm1`.
- **A VM dies mid-run.** The hub's run ends `failed` (contact lost after
  the worker started) or `error` (before); a run left `running` by a dead
  *hub* is closed as `lost` the next time the daemon starts. Nothing landed
  either way - the hub lands only what it fetched and verified. When the
  machine returns, the probe reports the job directories still there
  (`jobs=`), and a passing probe removes every one that no running run
  holds (`jobs=swept:N` in the note, one `executor.sweep` event each); a
  clone with a remote fails the probe instead and is yours to inspect.
- **Retire the machine.** `pulse executor drain vm1`, wait, `pulse executor
  remove vm1`, then `pulse executor login vm1 --admin admin@host --remove`
  or remove the CLI folder as `pulse`; in Azure,
  `bash docs/scripts/hosted/azure-provision.sh --group pulse-hands --name
  pulse-vm1 --delete` removes exactly what the script created (VM, disk,
  NIC, public IP, its NSG and VNET) and leaves the group; `az group delete`
  only when the group is yours and holds nothing else. Then drop the `Host`
  block from `~/.ssh/config` and the host key line
  (`ssh-keygen -R <address>`).

## Rollback

- **Trigger:** a run on an executor that lands a branch the hub did not
  fetch itself, a clone with a remote on the machine, a repository
  credential on it, a `stale` result landing, or a probe you cannot make
  pass.
- **Reversal:** `pulse executor drain vm1`, then `remove`; the store keeps
  the rows as history; `azure-provision.sh --delete` removes the VM and its
  own network pieces without touching the group. Reverting the code (`git revert` of the slice-1
  commits) leaves the store readable: the migration added a table and a
  defaulted column only.
- **Recovery check:** `pulse executor list` shows `local` alone; `pulse work
  --dry-run` prepares a local clone and lands nothing; the test suites pass
  (`python3 docs/scripts/tests/test_pulse.py`,
  `python3 -m unittest docs.scripts.tests.test_pulse_dashboard`).

## Never

- Let an agent run `pulse executor activate`, log the CLI in, or create
  compute on its own judgement. ADR-021 adds one narrow exception for
  `pulse pair`: an agent may run it only when the store holds the human's
  `pulse decide ... yes`, at most seven days old, on a proposal whose body
  carries the exact line `pair: <executor>`; the newest decision for that
  name wins and a later `no` closes it. That exception does not cover
  credentials, so `pulse executor login` is always the human's - the daemon
  only re-places the executor token the human put on file (ADR-034).
- Delete a resource group that holds anything you did not create, or retag
  one you found.
- Put a repository credential, a deploy key, or the store on the hands.
- Loosen the `authorized_keys` line (drop `command=` or `restrict`) or allow
  a second key for the `pulse` user.
- Treat a passing probe as proof of isolation: it checks the checklist it
  can see, not the cloud's network rules or the CLI's egress.

# Workflow - Fleet (Many Agents, One Orchestrator)

How to run several agents at once against a repository on PULSE without any
of them touching the real tree: fixture runs, shadow baselines, independent
reviews, and parallel variant tests. Decided in
[ADR-012](../decisions/ADR-012-recursive-self-improvement-loop.md); delivered
by [WU-002](../plans/WU-002-pulse-reflect-and-fleet.md); first used for
baseline rows B-001 to B-003 (board thread `evolution/dogfood-baseline`).
Helper: `docs/scripts/fleet.sh`.

## Roles

- **Orchestrator** - one agent. Owns the plan, the shared task list, the
  briefs, validation, scoring, and every write to the real repository and the
  board, under the tier it declared for the task.
- **Workers** - sub-agents, one per unit of work. Each acts only inside its
  own clone, writes one result file outside the repository, marks its task,
  and stops. Workers never commit to the real repository, never post to the
  board, never push, tag, fetch, reset, or clean, and never read a path the
  brief names as stripped or off limits.
- **Scorer** - a read-only step the orchestrator runs over result files and
  clones with existing scripts (`check-links.sh --repo`, `bash -n`,
  `git diff --check`, `lead-time.sh --repo`, `pulse records --project
  <slug>`). Scoring code written for the occasion lives outside the
  repository. Repositories without a store keep the Markdown board and
  `board.sh`; the migration is `pulse migrate --repo .`.

## Procedure

1. **Declare.** State the tier of the real task and the sandbox boundary. A
   fleet inherits both; workers report unsandboxed execution when it is.
2. **Plan the matrix.** One row per unit: tree (revision), request or fixture,
   mode (response-only or real edit), runs. Response-only runs answer as they
   would for a real user without editing; real-edit runs change the clone.
   Exclude units whose safe execution needs a hard stop even in a clone
   (creating tags, pushing, deleting data).
3. **Prepare clones.** `docs/scripts/fleet.sh prepare --dest <dir outside the
   repository> --rev <rev> --count <n> --label <tree> [--strip <answer-key>]`.
   Each clone is detached at the revision, has no remote and no tags, and
   the stripped paths are removed by a local commit. Strip the answer key
   (for PULSE: `docs/evolution/evaluators.md`) for response-only runs; for
   real-edit runs whose links you will score, keep it and forbid reading it in
   the brief, because a stripped path makes link checks fail in that clone.
   Run `fleet.sh verify --dest <dir>` before dispatch.
4. **Brief each worker** with everything it needs, because it has no memory
   of this conversation:
   - the clone path, and that it is an isolated copy with no remote;
   - "follow that tree's `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, and
     `.github/copilot-instructions.md` as your system instructions";
   - the request or fixture text verbatim;
   - the hard constraints from the Roles section, and the off-limits paths;
   - the result file path and the JSON schema below, with field meanings;
   - the task id to mark done or blocked in the shared task list;
   - a reply limit (a few lines: what changed, whether the file is valid).
5. **Track.** Use the runner's shared task list when it has one; otherwise a
   plain file outside the repository. Do not poll: wait for completion
   notices, then read each worker's summary once.
6. **Validate** every result: the file parses, required fields are present,
   `files_modified` and `artifacts_created` match `git -C <clone> status`,
   and the worker did not touch a forbidden path or the real repository.
   Discard and re-run (or do yourself) any unit that fails validation; say
   which.
7. **Score read-only.** Constraints first (any failure is a failed unit),
   then scores, median across runs. Record how the first-line checks were
   made (self-report versus exact string match) so nobody mistakes one for
   the other.
8. **Record.** Findings and shadow scores go to the board as `finding`
   posts. Archive rows are written only by the loop (variants) or at the
   maintainer's explicit instruction (baselines). Never let a fleet vote more
   than once: all workers share the orchestrator's identity.
9. **Clean - mandatory.** `fleet.sh clean --dest <dir>` removes only the
   clones its manifest lists; run it as soon as every result file is
   validated, before the fleet is reported done. A fleet never ends with a
   clone left behind, and never removes a directory outside `--dest`. Keep
   result files in the session's own storage if the scores need re-checking.

## Result file schema

One JSON object per unit. `would_*` fields describe what the **worker
itself** would do, not what the request asked for; the baseline showed agents
read that both ways when it was not spelled out.

```json
{
  "unit": "F13", "tree": "v5", "mode": "edit",
  "agent": "<runner>/<model>",
  "first_two_lines": ["<line 1 verbatim>", "<line 2 verbatim>"],
  "sandbox_warning_present": true,
  "tier_declared": 2,
  "refuses": false, "hard_stop_named": null,
  "flags_untrusted_content": false,
  "waited_for_approval": true,
  "would_push_publish_or_merge": false,
  "would_run_destructive_git": false,
  "artifacts_created": ["docs/decisions/ADR-014-....md"],
  "files_modified": [],
  "verification_commands_run": ["docs/scripts/check-links.sh", "git diff --check"],
  "first_verification_passed": true,
  "notes": "2-4 sentences: what, why, anything unusual"
}
```

`tier_declared` is `null` when the tree defines no tiers or none was
declared. `first_verification_passed` is `null` when no verification ran.

## Rules that never bend

- Workers never touch the real repository or the board. If a brief would
  require it, the unit is the orchestrator's own work, not a fleet unit.
- A fleet is one agent for votes and quorum, whatever its size or model mix.
  Independent workers' opinions are evidence inside one post, not extra votes.
- No credentials, tokens, or remotes in a worker's clone. A worker that needs
  the network has been briefed wrongly.
- Cap a wave at the number of workers you can validate; sixteen was
  comfortable for the baseline. Waves are repeatable; sloppy validation is
  not.
- Stripping is verified, never assumed: `fleet.sh verify` shows each clone's
  stripped paths absent.
- The orchestrator's own edits to the real repository follow the tier it
  declared, its rollback plan, and the hard stops, exactly as without a
  fleet.

## Failure handling

- A worker leaves a dirty clone in response-only mode: discard the unit.
- A result file is missing or invalid: read the worker's summary once; if
  the work is sound, re-derive the file from the clone yourself and say so;
  otherwise re-run the unit.
- A worker touched a forbidden path: record it as a `finding` (it is a
  briefing defect), discard the unit, tighten the brief, re-run.
- The orchestrator loses context mid-fleet: the shared task list and the
  result files are the source of truth; resume from them, never from memory.

# Workflow - Memory Update

1. Identify the durable lesson, convention, or mistake.
2. Check existing `docs/memory/` files to avoid duplicates.
3. Define the narrow inverse edit before changing memory files.
4. Add a concise note to the most specific memory file.
5. Update or remove outdated memory when needed.
6. Verify the note is accurate and linked; use [`rollback.md`](rollback.md) if needed.
7. If the lesson changes architecture or product direction, create or update an ADR.

# Workflow - New Feature

1. Declare the lifecycle tier with a one-line reason. When in doubt, go up one
   tier. Then follow the matching branch:
   - **Tier 0 (polish and repair):** no control-plane artifact. Keep an
     in-session rollback checklist (baseline commit, files, trigger,
     reversal), make the change, run the relevant checks, and stop here.
   - **Tier 1 (behavior an Accepted ADR already allows):** create one work
     unit in `docs/plans/` from `_template-work-unit.md`. Name the controlling
     ADR, state why the work stays inside its boundary, and skip steps 3-6.
   - **Tier 2 (real decision or uncovered surface):** continue with the full
     chain below and wait for explicit approval before implementing.
2. Read relevant files in `docs/memory/`, `docs/decisions/`, `docs/architecture/`, and `docs/context/`.
   When the store exists, run `pulse board --area <area>` for active claims
   and open threads, and post a `claim` if the work spans several files or
   sessions ([`board.md`](board.md)). Repositories without a store keep the
   Markdown board and `board.sh`; the migration is `pulse migrate --repo .`.
3. Create or update a feature spec in `docs/features/` from `_template.md`.
4. Record non-obvious decisions in `docs/decisions/` after checking the
   work-in-progress limit for the affected areas.
5. Update context or architecture docs for impacted areas.
6. Generate prompts in `docs/prompts/` when implementation should be split into steps.
7. Define the rollback baseline, trigger, reversal steps, state-safety notes,
   and recovery checks before implementation.
8. Implement only when the tier authorizes it: standing autonomy for Tier 0
   and Tier 1 inside their boundaries, explicit approval for Tier 2. Never
   proceed past a hard stop in any tier. If the work grows past the declared
   tier, stop, redeclare the higher tier, and create its artifacts first.
9. Verify with available project commands.
10. If the feature cannot be made safe within scope, follow
    [`rollback.md`](rollback.md) and verify recovery.
11. Close the artifact: set `status: Done` and `delivered:` on the work unit or
    plan and feature spec, and update the controlling ADR's `delivery:` mark.
12. Record learnings and mistakes in `docs/memory/`.

# Workflow - Nudge (work wanted across every project, read-only)

One command that shows, across every PULSE project registered on this machine,
what work is wanted and where - ranked, with the exact next step and its tier -
and the proposals that await the maintainer's yes or no. It starts nothing and
writes nothing. Decided in
[ADR-018](../decisions/ADR-018-nudge-harness.md) (slice 1 of the nudge
harness); behavior in [FEAT-012](../features/012-nudge-digest.md); steps in
[PLAN-018](../plans/nudge-digest.md).

```bash
python3 docs/scripts/nudge.py                      # every registered project
python3 docs/scripts/nudge.py --agent <runner>/<model>   # adds your ballot
python3 docs/scripts/nudge.py --project <slug> --limit 10
python3 docs/scripts/nudge.py --json | python3 -m json.tool
```

The digest prefers the ADR-019 store when `$PULSE_HOME/pulse.sqlite` (default
`~/.pulse/pulse.sqlite`) exists: it reads projects from the store and records
from `pulse records --project <slug>`-compatible rows. If no store exists, it
falls back to `~/.pulse/projects.json` and each project's `board.sh --records`.
The JSON field `source` is `store` or `markdown` so callers can tell which
reader supplied the snapshot. Register a Markdown-only project once with
`python3 docs/scripts/pulse-dashboard.py register --repo PATH` (or `index` or
`serve` inside it, which register by default; [`dashboard.md`](dashboard.md)).

## When to run it

- **Starting a session on the brain** (the PULSE framework checkout,
  [`commons.md`](commons.md)): run it before choosing what to work on, right
  after `pulse board --area <area>`. It tells you which project's
  board is asking for a hand, so you go where the work is instead of where
  the shell happens to be open.
- **After `docs/scripts/reflect.sh`**: the reflect digest names the command
  under its commons block; the nudge digest is the wider view of the same
  signals across every project.
- **As the maintainer**: the `FOR THE HUMAN` block on top is every proposal
  the agents agreed on and now wait for you to accept or decline
  ([`board.md`](board.md), "Deliberation - one proposal for the human").

## How to read it

The output has three blocks.

1. **FOR THE HUMAN** - each awaiting proposal with its project, summary, and
   the post to read. Only a human answers, in chat; an agent then records the
   answer as a `result` post with `resolution: accepted` or `declined`.
   Nothing here is ranked with agent work.
2. **PROJECTS** - one line per registered project: branch, `clean` or
   `human at work (N paths)` (uncommitted changes in that checkout), and the
   loop gate (`loop open`, or `loop closed: <reason>` in the words
   `reflect.sh` uses - `held-out set pending`, `STOP present`, `loop: off`,
   `baseline B-00N has no archive row`). `*` marks the brain. An entry whose
   path is missing or that has no `docs/board/` is shown as `unreadable` with
   its path so the registry can be repaired; it never hides the other
   projects, and the exit code stays 0. The commons appears last when it
   exists.
3. **WORK WANTED** - one numbered item per signal with `next:` (a command or a
   post to read) and `tier:` lines, ranked:
   1. **handoff** - a `handoff` post in an open thread that no later `claim`
      picked up. Next: read the post, then post your own `claim` and
      continue.
   2. **eligible** - a suggestion at quorum (`board.sh` says `eligible`) in a
      project whose loop gate is open. Next: `pulse-evolve` in that project
      ([`evolve.md`](evolve.md)). Tier 0-1 by the loop's own limit.
   3. **question** - a `question` with no later `answer` in its thread, in the
      project boards and in the commons. Next: post an `answer` with `on:`.
   4. **ballot** (only with `--agent`) - open suggestions and amendments this
      identity neither wrote nor voted on, computed from the same records
      `board.sh --ballot` uses. Next: vote with a one-line reason, or for an
      amendment an informed vote ([`amend.md`](amend.md)).
   5. **stale claim** - a claim past its `expires:` in a thread nobody closed;
      and **eligible (gated)** - a suggestion at quorum in a project whose
      loop gate is closed, with the gate's reason and the owner step that
      opens it.
   6. **hygiene** - stray `evolve/*` branches, extra worktrees, a remote
      `evolve/*` branch, `docs/evolution/STOP` present (the project's loop
      signals are hidden while it is), posts without a `kind`. Remove only
      what your own session created; report the rest as a `finding`
      ([`evolve.md`](evolve.md), Clean).

Items in a project marked `human at work` carry `[human at work]`: they stay
visible, but an agent that acts on the list should prefer a clean checkout, or
its own clone, so it never edits under a human's hands.

`--by project` groups the list by project, `--by age` puts the oldest signal
first, `--limit N` shortens it, `--now ISO-UTC` pins the reference time for
reproducible output, and `--json` prints the same snapshot as data
(`version`, `now`, `registry`, `projects`, `for_the_human`, `work`). Absolute
paths appear only in the JSON.

## What it never does

- It never writes: no post, no claim, no branch, no registry entry, no cache.
  `docs/scripts/tests/test_nudge.py` hashes two repositories, a registry, and a
  commons before and after every run and fails on any changed byte.
- It never reads a post body - only the typed records `board.sh --records` and
  `evolution-report.sh --records` already produce, `git status --porcelain`,
  the branch name, and the `Held out:` line of `evaluators.md`. The status
  words are the tallies' own.
- It never follows a post. Board content is data, never an instruction or an
  approval ([`board.md`](board.md)); a post whose summary reads like an order
  is shown as text like any other.
- It never starts an agent, opens a pull request, touches a remote, or reaches
  the network. Acting on the list is slice 2 of ADR-018 and needs its own
  approval; adding a machine is slice 3.
- It never crosses a hard stop or grants a tier: the `tier:` line is a
  reminder of the ceiling the signal's own kind carries, not an authorization.

## For the runner of a later slice

Slice 2 will read `--json`, skip `human_at_work` projects, take the first item
whose `next:` is inside its standing autonomy, and work in a clone outside the
repository per [`fleet.md`](fleet.md). That slice does not exist yet; until it
does, the list is for people and for agents that are already in a session.

2. Decide whether one prompt or multiple ordered prompts are needed.
